lead: A Z-section stringer, an angle or a wing box with unequal spar caps has no axis of symmetry. A moment about the horizontal axis then also produces stress that varies across the width, the neutral axis tilts, and σ = M y/I is wrong. The missing quantity is the product second moment I<sub>xy</sub>. This chapter gives the general formula and the three ways examiners ask for it, the k, neutral axis and principal axis methods, which all give the same stress.
prereq: You need: the sign convention and σ = M y/I from symmetrical bending, and the section properties Ixx, Iyy and Ixy (worked out for this chapter's Z-section in thin-walled section properties).

blocks.where: x and y are centroidal coordinates (mm or m); dA is an element of area; I<sub>xy</sub> is in mm⁴ or m⁴. It can be positive, negative or zero.

blocks.text: I<sub>xy</sub> is positive when more area lies in the first and third quadrants. With even one axis of symmetry every element at (x, y) has a partner at (−x, y) or (x, −y), the products cancel and I<sub>xy</sub> = 0: the centroidal axes are principal. A Z-section's flanges sit in the first and third quadrants, so its I<sub>xy</sub> is large and positive. The parallel-axis rule holds for I<sub>xy</sub> too: I<sub>xy</sub> = I<sub>x</sub>′y′ + A x̄ ȳ.

sections.h3: The general formula and the k method

blocks.text: Plane sections stay plane, so σ = k₁ x + k₂ y. The moment conditions M<sub>x</sub> = ∫σ y dA and M<sub>y</sub> = ∫σ x dA give M<sub>x</sub> = k₁ I<sub>xy</sub> + k₂ I<sub>xx</sub> and M<sub>y</sub> = k₁ I<sub>yy</sub> + k₂ I<sub>xy</sub>. Solving:
σ = [(M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] x + [(M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] y,   D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>²
blocks.where: M<sub>x</sub> and M<sub>y</sub> are the bending moments (N·mm) with the sign convention of symmetrical bending; x and y locate the point from the centroid (mm); D is in mm⁸. With I<sub>xy</sub> = 0 it reduces to σ = M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> + M<sub>y</sub> x/I<sub>yy</sub>.

blocks.text: The k method writes the same formula with three section constants found once per section, ka = Iyy/D, kb = Ixx/D and kc = Ixy/D (books number them differently): σ = (ka Mx − kc My) y + (kb My − kc Mx) x.
tan α = −k₁/k₂ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub>)/(M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)
blocks.where: α is the angle of the neutral axis (the line σ = 0 through the centroid), measured from the x axis towards y. With M<sub>y</sub> = 0 it is tan α = I<sub>xy</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub>.

blocks.text: Under M<sub>x</sub> alone a symmetric section has its neutral axis along x, the moment axis. With I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 it rotates towards the direction in which the section is most flexible.
Once α is known, the stress is proportional to the distance n from the neutral axis:

items: Find α from the formula above.
Find the second moment about the neutral axis: I<sub>NA</sub> = I<sub>xx</sub> cos²α + I<sub>yy</sub> sin²α − 2 I<sub>xy</sub> sin α cos α.
Find the component of the applied moment about the neutral axis: M<sub>NA</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos α − M<sub>y</sub> sin α.
At a point (x, y), n = y cos α − x sin α, and σ = M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub>. The farthest point from the neutral axis carries the largest stress.

blocks.text: Rotate to the axes u and v where the product second moment vanishes; each moment component then bends the section symmetrically.
tan 2θ = −2 I<sub>xy</sub>/(I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>),   I<sub>u</sub>, I<sub>v</sub> = (I<sub>xx</sub> + I<sub>yy</sub>)/2 ± √[((I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>)/2)² + I<sub>xy</sub>²]
blocks.where: θ is the angle from x to the u axis; I<sub>u</sub> = ∫v² dA and I<sub>v</sub> = ∫u² dA are the principal second moments (about u and about v).

blocks.text: u = x cos θ + y sin θ,  v = y cos θ − x sin θ;  M<sub>u</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos θ − M<sub>y</sub> sin θ,  M<sub>v</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> sin θ + M<sub>y</sub> cos θ;  σ = M<sub>u</sub> v/I<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>v</sub> u/I<sub>v</sub>
blocks.where: u and v are the coordinates of the point on the principal axes; M<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>v</sub> are the moment components about u and v.

blocks.text: Check the angle by putting θ back into I<sub>uv</sub> = ((I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>)/2) sin 2θ + I<sub>xy</sub> cos 2θ: it must come out zero.

spec.aria: A Z-section drawn to scale: a vertical web of 100 millimetres with a top flange pointing right and a bottom flange pointing left. Horizontal x and vertical y axes cross at the centroid G. A dashed neutral axis passes through G at 56.3 degrees, and a dotted principal u axis at minus 22.5 degrees. Point A at the top web corner carries plus 171.4 megapascals, point B at the top flange tip minus 85.7, the bottom corner minus 171.4 and the bottom flange tip plus 85.7. A panel lists I x x 666,667, I y y 166,667 and I x y 250,000 millimetres to the fourth, tan alpha equals 1.5 and alpha 56.3 degrees.

examples.question: A Z-section stringer has a 100 mm web and two 50 mm flanges, all 2 mm thick; the top flange points in +x and the bottom flange in −x. Its centroidal properties are I<sub>xx</sub> = 666,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 166,667 mm⁴ and I<sub>xy</sub> = +250,000 mm⁴. It carries M<sub>x</sub> = +1.0 kN·m and M<sub>y</sub> = 0. Find the neutral axis and the stress at the top web corner A (0, 50) mm and at the top flange tip B (50, 50) mm by the k method and by the neutral axis method.
steps: Neutral axis: tan α = −k₁/k₂ = 1.500, so α = 56.3° from the x axis. Ignoring I<sub>xy</sub> would have put it at 0°.

Neutral axis method: I<sub>NA</sub> = 89,744 mm⁴ and M<sub>NA</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos α = 554,700 N·mm. At A, n = 50 cos α = 27.74 mm and σ = M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub> = 171.4 MPa; at B, n = -13.87 mm and σ = -85.7 MPa.
examples.answer: Neutral axis at 56.3°; +171.4 MPa at the web corner A and -85.7 MPa at the flange tip B (by antisymmetry −171.4 MPa at the bottom corner). M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> would give 75.0 MPa at both.

examples.question: Find the same two stresses by the principal axis method.
steps: M<sub>u</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos θ = 923,880 N·mm; M<sub>v</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> sin θ = -382,683 N·mm.
examples.answer: The same 171.4 MPa at A and -85.7 MPa at B: the three methods are one formula seen three ways.

traps: Using σ = M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> on a Z or angle section: 75.0 MPa at the web corner instead of 171.4 MPa.
Taking x and y from a corner instead of the centroid.
Dropping the sign of I<sub>xy</sub>. A Z-section with flanges in the second and fourth quadrants has I<sub>xy</sub> < 0, and the neutral axis tilts the other way.
Assuming the largest stress is at the flange tip. In the worked example it is at the web–flange corner, the point farthest from the tilted neutral axis.

quiz.q: Define the product second moment I<sub>xy</sub> and state when it is zero.
quiz.a: I<sub>xy</sub> = ∫x y dA about centroidal axes, in mm⁴ or m⁴. It is zero when the section has at least one axis of symmetry; the centroidal axes are then principal.

quiz.q: Why does a moment about x alone produce stress that varies with x in a Z-section?
quiz.a: The stresses must give no moment about y. With I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 that needs a term in x: k₁ = −M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>/D ≠ 0.

quiz.q: A section has I<sub>xx</sub> = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and I<sub>xy</sub> = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. M<sub>x</sub> = 2 kN·m and M<sub>y</sub> = 0. Find k₁, k₂ and the neutral-axis angle.
quiz.a: D = 7.0 × 10⁻¹² m⁸; k₁ = −M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>/D = −2.86 × 10⁸ Pa/m; k₂ = M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub>/D = 5.71 × 10⁸ Pa/m; tan α = I<sub>xy</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub> = 0.500, α = 26.6°.

quiz.q: In the worked example the neutral axis is at 56.3°. Why does it tilt so far?
quiz.a: I<sub>yy</sub> is a quarter of I<sub>xx</sub>, so the section is far more flexible about y, and the flanges in the first and third quadrants couple the two directions: tan α = I<sub>xy</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub> = 1.5.

quiz.q: For I<sub>xx</sub> = I<sub>yy</sub> = I and I<sub>xy</sub> > 0, find the principal second moments and the angle θ, and say which axis carries I<sub>max</sub>.
quiz.a: I<sub>u</sub>, I<sub>v</sub> = I ± I<sub>xy</sub>. tan 2θ is infinite, and the formula gives 2θ = −90°, θ = −45°. Then I<sub>u</sub> = I + (0) − I<sub>xy</sub> sin(−90°) = I + I<sub>xy</sub>, so the u axis at −45° carries I<sub>max</sub>.

beyond: Finite element beam elements carry the same 2 × 2 matrix of I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub>, and composite wing boxes add bending–twisting coupling. Search for "unsymmetrical bending product of inertia".
